facts.statement: Anchisaurus lived during the Early Jurassic Period, approximately 200 to 192 million years ago, in what is now the Northeastern United States.
facts.quote: It lived during the Early Jurassic Period, and its fossils have been found in the red sandstone of the Upper Portland Formation, Northeastern United States, which was deposited from the Hettangian age into the Sinemurian age, between about 200 and 192 million years ago.

facts.statement: Sauropodomorph remains were first found in North America in 1818 in East Windsor, Connecticut, when Solomon Ellsworth Jr. uncovered bones nearly 6 feet long while digging a well.
facts.quote: Sauropodomorph remains were first documented in North America in 1818, when some bones nearly 6 ft in length were uncovered by Mr. Solomon Ellsworth Jr. while excavating a well with gunpowder in East Windsor, Connecticut.

facts.statement: When first discovered, the bones were initially mistaken for human remains until tail vertebrae proved otherwise.
facts.quote: At the time of their discovery it was thought that the bones might be those of a human, but the presence of tail vertebrae falsified that idea.

facts.statement: The original type specimen of Anchisaurus polyzelus was discovered in 1855 by William Smith in Springfield, Massachusetts, while blasting a well for the Springfield Armory.
facts.quote: In 1855, the original type specimen of Anchisaurus polyzelus, AM 41/109, which is housed at the Amherst College Museum of Natural History, was found by William Smith in Springfield, Massachusetts during blasting a well for the waterhouse at the Springfield Armory.

facts.statement: Edward Hitchcock Jr. described the Springfield remains in 1863, suggesting they were the source of mysterious reptile tracks his father had studied.
facts.quote: In 1863, the son of the ichnologist Edward Hitchcock, Edward Hitchcock Jr, described the Springfield remains in a supplement to his father's work on fossil footprints, suggesting they could explain a certain mysterious kind of reptile tracks.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh renamed the genus Anchisaurus in 1885 after finding that previous names were already in use, keeping the meaning 'near lizard'.
facts.quote: In 1885, Marsh had discovered that this name also had been preoccupied, by the anthracosaurian Amphisaurus Barkas 1870, and again replaced it by Anchisaurus, with the same meaning.

facts.statement: In 2015, the ICZN designated the type specimen of A. colurus as the neotype for the genus Anchisaurus, making A. polyzelus and A. colurus objective synonyms.
facts.quote: In 2015, the ICZN formally made the more complete type specimen of A. colurus the neotype of the genus Anchisaurus and the species A. polyzelus, rendering A. polyzelus and A. colurus objective synonyms (both names being based on exactly the same fossil).

facts.statement: Bones from South Africa were originally named Gyposaurus capensis in 1911 but were renamed Anchisaurus capensis in 1976.
facts.quote: Broom named Gyposaurus capensis in 1911, from bones discovered in South Africa but Peter Galton renamed these Anchisaurus capensis in 1976.

facts.statement: Remains from the Navajo Sandstone in Arizona, which is the same age as the Portland Formation, have been referred to as Ammosaurus.
facts.quote: The Navajo Sandstone of Arizona is the same age as the Portland Formation, and has produced prosauropod remains that have been referred to as Ammosaurus.

facts.statement: Evidence of gastroliths and a small sphenodont skull suggests Anchisaurus was omnivorous, eating mostly plants but occasionally meat.
facts.quote: A large number of gastroliths, stones swallowed to grind up plant material in the gut, were found in the abdomen, as well as bone from the skull of a small sphenodont, Clevosaurus. This indicates that these dinosaurs were omnivorous, with a diet mainly consisting of plants but with an occasional supplement of meat.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus was a small dinosaur measuring just over 2 meters in length, which contributed to early confusion with human bones.
facts.quote: Anchisaurus was a rather small dinosaur, with a length of just over 2 m, which helps explain why it was once mistaken for human bones.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus probably weighed around 27 kilograms.
facts.quote: It probably weighed around 27 kg.

facts.statement: The species A. major was larger, measuring between 2.5 and 4 meters and weighing up to 70 pounds.
facts.quote: However, Marsh's species A. major (also known as Ammosaurus) was larger, from 2.5 to 4 m and some estimates give it a weight of up to 70 lb.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Anchisaurus to be 2.2 meters long and weigh 20 kilograms in 2010.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 2.2 m and its weight at 20 kg in 2010.

facts.statement: Yates estimated that Anchisaurus could measure up to 4.9 meters in length based on four known specimens.
facts.quote: Based on the four known specimens of Anchisaurus, Yates estimated that the animal measured up to 4.9 m in length.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus is classified as a genus of basal sauropodomorph dinosaur.
facts.quote: Anchisaurus is a genus of basal sauropodomorph dinosaur.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus was previously classified as a member of Prosauropoda.
facts.quote: Until recently it was classed as a member of Prosauropoda.

facts.statement: Recent studies show that Anchisaurus is closer to sauropods than to traditional prosauropods.
facts.quote: Recent investigations show that a group of traditional prosauropods form a monophyletic sister-group to Sauropoda, and that Anchisaurus is instead closer to sauropods.

facts.statement: The family Anchisauridae was proposed by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1885 to include Anchisaurus and its nearest relatives.
facts.quote: The family Anchisauridae was first proposed by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1885 and later defined as a clade consisting of Anchisaurus and its nearest relatives.

facts.statement: The family Anchisauridae is not widely used in current taxonomies because it is unclear which genera belong to it.
facts.quote: However, it is not clear which other genera are included in the family; many of the dinosaurs once included have since been moved elsewhere, and the group is not used in most current taxonomies.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Nova Scotia remains belong to Anchisaurus or represent a new taxon, Fendusaurus eldoni, though they suggest an omnivorous diet.
facts.quote: The Nova Scotia material provides clues about the diet of these animals. A large number of gastroliths, stones swallowed to grind up plant material in the gut, were found in the abdomen, as well as bone from the skull of a small sphenodont, Clevosaurus. This indicates that these dinosaurs were omnivorous, with a diet mainly consisting of plants but with an occasional supplement of meat. However, these remains have never been fully described or illustrated and were only tentatively referred to Ammosaurus. A further study identified them as a new taxon of sauropodomorph, Fendusaurus eldoni.

facts.statement: Fossils of Anchisaurus were first found in the Portland Formation of the Newark Supergroup in the Connecticut River Valley.
facts.quote: Fossils of Anchisaurus were originally discovered in the Portland Formation of the Newark Supergroup in the Connecticut River Valley.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus lived in an arid environment with distinct wet and dry seasons between 200 and 195 million years ago.
facts.quote: This formation preserves an arid environment with strong wet and dry seasons, from the Hettangian age into the Sinemurian age, between about 200 and 195 million years ago.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus swallowed gastroliths to aid in digesting plant matter.
facts.quote: This herbivore swallowed gastroliths (gizzard stones) to help break down the food in its stomach.

facts.statement: The spoon-shaped teeth of Anchisaurus were adapted for ripping food.
facts.quote: Anchisaurus teeth, used to rip food, were shaped like spoons.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus had fewer, more widely spaced teeth and narrower feet compared to true prosauropods.
facts.quote: It had fewer and more widely spaced teeth than true prosauropods, and as Peter Galton and Michael Cluver observed, narrower feet.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus could turn its front legs inward to use them as grasping hands.
facts.quote: As 'hands', they could be turned inwards and be used for grasping.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus had five toes on its feet that could be placed flat against the ground with strong ankles.
facts.quote: As feet, the five toes could be placed flat against the floor and were strong at the ankle.

facts.statement: Multiple Anchisaurus specimens are preserved as partially articulated skeletons despite being found in a high-energy river environment that typically scatters bones.
facts.quote: Notably, multiple specimens of Anchisaurus are preserved as partially articulated skeletons, despite these specimens being preserved in a high-energy riverine environment that would have disarticulated the bones.

facts.statement: The genus Anchisaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1885.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1885

facts.statement: The only known species of Anchisaurus is A. polyzelus.
facts.quote: species: A. polyzelus

facts.statement: Anchisaurus polyzelus has several synonyms including Megadactylus polyzelus, Amphisaurus polyzelus, and Thecodontosaurus polyzelus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Megadactylus polyzelus Hitchcock, 1865 Amphisaurus polyzelus Marsh, 1882 Anchisaurus colurus Marsh, 1891 Anchisaurus solus Marsh, 1892 Yaleosaurus colurus Huene, 1932 Thecodontosaurus polyzelus Fedak and Galton 2007

facts.statement: The name Anchisaurus was coined as a replacement for Amphisaurus, which itself replaced Megadactylus, both of which had previously been used for other animals.
facts.quote: Anchisaurus fue acuñado como un nombre de reemplazo para Amphisaurus , que era en sí mismo un nombre de reemplazo para Megadactylus de Hitchcock, ambos de los cuales ya habían sido utilizadas para otros animales.

facts.statement: In 1884, nearly complete specimens found in Manchester, Connecticut, served as templates for O.C. Marsh to restore the skeleton.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus likely spent most of its time on four legs but could stand up on its hind legs to reach higher plants.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists debate whether Anchisaurus may have also eaten meat, given its position in the transition between herbivorous and carnivorous groups.

facts.statement: There is still some discussion regarding the diet of Anchisaurus.

facts.statement: Anchisaurus had a large thumb claw and large eyes that were not entirely on the sides of the skull, unlike a typical prey animal.

facts.statement: The first discovery of Anchisaurus predates the description of any other dinosaur and is possibly the first known dinosaur from North America.
facts.quote: El primer descubrimiento de Anchisaurus es anterior a la descripción de cualquier otro dinosaurio, y es posiblemente el primer dinosauro conocido de Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The presence of tail bones led researchers to recognize the fossils as belonging to an indeterminate sauropodomorph, possibly closely related to prosauropods like Plateosaurus.
